title: About Heat and Your Health

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: If you are outside, especially for a long time, and the HeatRisk is red or above, you can:

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Stay in the shade as much as possible.

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Take breaks when you can.

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Do outdoor activities during the coolest parts of the day or evening, if possible.

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: When you are indoors, you can:

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Use fans, but only if indoor temperatures are less than 90°F. In temperatures above 90°F, a fan can increase body temperature.

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Use air conditioning or find a location that has one by dialing 2-1-1, visiting the National Center for Healthy Housing's Cooling Centers by State page, or by contacting your local health department or emergency management agency.

sections.heading: Stay Cool
sections.text: Check on your family, friends, and neighbors, especially if they have chronic medical problems or live alone. Check on pets.

sections.heading: Stay Hydrated
sections.text: Drink plenty of fluids

sections.heading: Stay Hydrated
sections.text: Carry a water bottle. Drink and refill it throughout the day.

sections.heading: Stay Hydrated
sections.text: Consider limiting beverages high in sugars and sodium, caffeine, and alcohol.

sections.heading: Stay Hydrated
sections.text: Check your urine color. When it's light yellow or clear, it usually means you are drinking enough water.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: If your body gets too hot, you can get sick. Know the symptoms of your body overheating and know when to seek medical care.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Symptoms can include:

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Muscle cramping

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Unusually heavy sweating

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Shortness of breath

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Dizziness

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Headaches

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Weakness

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Nausea

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Check your local HeatRisk and Air Quality

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Enter your zip code on the CDC HeatRisk Dashboard for the heat risk forecast in your area and take recommended actions to protect your health.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Plus, check air quality levels – so you can plan your week with your health in mind.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Have a plan for your medicine

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Many medicines can make you dehydrated or overheated on hot days. Also, some medicines need to be kept out of hot places.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Don't stop or change your medicines until you talk to your doctor.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Heat can cause power outages. Have a plan for what to do with refrigerated medications and electronic medical devices.

sections.heading: Know the Symptoms
sections.text: Store your medicines properly- some may need to be kept out of hot places.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: Although anyone at any time can suffer from heat-related illness, some people are at greater risk than others. Check on your family, friends, and neighbors, especially if they live alone or have chronic medical problems.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: Some groups may have to take additional action on hot days, including:

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: People, especially children, with asthma.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: People with heart disease.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: Pregnant women.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: People 65 years of age or older.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: People who are working or exercising outside in the heat.

sections.heading: For Those at High Risk
sections.text: Infants and young children.
